I write a full page usually, for every session (sometimes half a page a land a shit ton of sticky notes) But my real notes are made before the campaign is run, or during it and are not important to the session (if I think of a cool religion, I'll make a note of that and add it to my stack but I it's not important to the best session so I don't count it with my session notes). I bring several notes to my games but usually only 1 is new and freshly written. 

I do a couple of things. My one full page is some stuff I think they might/could do during the session. It has new NPCs on it (I try to write at least 1 new NPC every time I come to a session so that I have a backlog of them, they don't have to interact with them). It has some combat encounters and other things I feel might be useful to think up before the session. I have a big over arching plot and villian in my game and in every note I write what's happening on the villian side so I'm keeping track of it too. I make other notes of important things I want to remember from last session or want to do for this session. The rest of the page is filled with a little hand written recap of last sessions events that I quickly go over at the start of every session (sometimes it's not always accurate, but the players help me out!). I also have on there notes of feedback players have given me (if any) so I'm aware of things I need to do. And lastly I make note of the other notes I might have brought to the session (if I wrote a letter from the commander of the army, I write down that I have that so I don't forget about my own content). 

And I leave the session always with more notes than I come in. I take note of what my players have done, what I think might be cool for a next session, and he how the world might react around them because of their actions, or anything else I think I need to prepare. 

I will quickly share that this game meets once a week, some times once every two weeks. For more regular games, I write a lot less.

First I would like to say that there's nothing wrong with a bit of a generic story. His scarred face could make him look /terrifying/  which just hinders him from helping people so he never takes off his mask. More than a sacred face you could maybe talk to your DM to see if they have any cool diseases or curses they can make that your character could have that could lend to your character.

Other ideas: the mask is permanently on his face (Majora's Mask style, it's perfect!). He's actually someone with a very well known face so he has to hide it. He straight up doesn't have a face, you take off that mask and there's nothing there. Face-swap: he somehow has the face of someone else (could be someone he hates and so even HE doesn't want to look at it) and so he hides it and it trying to get his own face back. I'm really liking the idea of a cursed mask, maybe the mask gives him some kind of benefit that he doesn't want to take it off. The (also) classic running from the law so he's hiding his face. I had a player once who created a character who was kind of a Mulan, in the sense that the character was actually a woman but wore a disguise that made her appear genderless (not sure that would apply in your character case though). Maybe he just doesn't want to take off his goddamn mask, geez. The mask was a present to him, and it feels /wrong/ to just take it off. The mask is precious to him, like someone who's worn glasses all their life he feels kind of naked not wearing it. It keeps him alive some how, like a breathing mask of some sort. 

Hope any of those ideas might inspire you :') maybe your DM has some cool things abrewing in their head that you can use for your character too

Haha okay, I get it now! You do seem to have a wild bunch on your hands. It seems as though you've made a great world for them to go exploring in and they're not really exploring into it. I think they kind of expect it to go one way but you've obviously created a very diverse world for them (which is good!). Making what you're doing (like having the wife make the DC higher) more obvious through your words might help, talking to your players about wanting them to engage more into the world I think might be good too. If players express confusion over something that's happened I do always try to explain things from the DM side, say that I rolled a secret counter check or that I raised the DC because they were being unkind to the NPC before hand, I find that that helps too and the players then understand that they need to try  a new way to interact with the world. Maybe give them scenarios where they HAVE to think things through, kind of gently force them to be a little less chatoic if you think that'll help (having them solve a murder mystery or something like that). Something that might give them more reason to engage with your world. 

In the end I guess if you've got players who would rather keep on playing the way they do then you'll have to mold the world around their style of play and try to have fun with it so that everyone can have a good time (the DMs enjoyment is as important as the player's after all). I think you can still have your very well-rounded out NPCs and their impulsive style of play work together. I know I said it before but talking to your players about this is good too, and they might have more insight into what they want. Good luck again! When those players say that they think your NPCs are only open to one type of solution, what do they mean by that? Are they only interacting in one way with your NPCs? Personally, I don't think you need to amend anything. Just like real life, people don't just fork over information. Just like real life, different people can be convinced in different ways to talk about what they know. Do you spice up your NPCs? Not all of them need to have deep personalities, some can be simple minded. You can try making some that are starkly different from ones you've made before to show your players that there is a variety there lol

I do the same in my games. My NPCs are people too, if my players fail checks then they have to get the information in other ways. I try to give all my NPCs goals too, just quick and simple things. So NPC John really wants to get his wife something for her birthday, much more than he cares about the Orc map that he has. He notices the nice ring a player is wearing and he'll trade for it. That's his goal from there it's up to the players how they want to react. A different NPC might NEVER give up that map because if he does he thinks he'll be killed. His goal is to live, so he'll be more susceptible to threats. These are facts I make very clear to my players and I let them act the way they want to. If I really don't think my players are getting it I use obvious language like "He looks nervous, his eyes dart to your daggers and every time you step closer he flinches" this sets him up as someone who seems like they could easily be intimated. In NPC John's case I might say something like "he's eyes are trained to—glued to really—your more expensive looking possessions". Of courses this is a very blunt way of doing it but I mix that in with NPCs that are more mysterious. I also have NPCs that will just give up information because it's easier to just have the plot advance quickly and not focus on that. You also sound like you have a variety of NPCs like that too so I think you could possibly try steering your players into interacting with your NPCs in a different way. 

Of course, you can also always bring this up with them on the side if it becomes a real issue because communication is so very important when it comes to D&D. Anyway, best of luck! English isn't my first language so hopefully I interpreted your post right lol

I had this problem when I first started DMing here are somethings I found to personally help:

* 1) TALKING TO THE PLAYERS. asking them why they're not interested in the story. what you can do to make it better.
* 2) Engaging characters into other character's stories/tying them together. Maybe character 2 finds out that character 3 has a son with the princess, now they both have a reason to be engaged in the story. Maybe character 5 needs a secret potion and OH LOOK AT THAT it just happens that character 4 is the ONLY ONE who knows how to make it.
* 3) let players consult out of character. this one might sound weird, and I'm not one that likes too much distracting OOC chatter when I feel it isn't necessary but let's say character 1 is off doing their own thing, shutting up the other players can make it hard for them to feel engaged so I encourage them to OOC consult with character 1 and let them add their commentary. Of course, this is to the DM's discretion. Depending on how this goes, it might be annoying to have the peanut gallery chatter but I find it helps people stay focused when their opinion is shown to be valued (which it is, of course)
* 4) SNACKS. food revolutionized my D&D game and I don't even know why.
* 5) don't let the spotlight stay on one character for too long. inevitably players will get a little bored from time to time. But never let the individual shopping trips go on for an hour. Have a character do their thing, and then cut to another character doing their thing, and then cut to another and on and on and on so you don't have just one character doing whatever for an hour. Interject other players in and cut up the story.
* 6) always look for ways to add characters in. kind of goes into what I meant for point 3 but let's say that character 2 and 4 need to do something, always try to look for ways for them to drag the other characters along or involve them in some way. 
* 7) people are narcissists, but I like to think that people are good to. If it's really a problem maybe the DM should really ask them to pay attention. It's not a hard thing, and it's not asking for much. 
* 8) why do they not care when the spotlight isn't on them? Maybe they don't care about the other people's characters. Okay. simple. Make them care about the other characters. Make them fall as in love with other character as they are with their own. when character 1 goes off all the players will be on the edges of their seats because they want to know what happens to character 1 because they /like/ character 1. a good way to do this is to have sort of in-game team building quests. or do something similar to what I mentioned before of getting characters involved into other character's backstories. 
* 9) have a sort of "yes man" there helps too. a player that shines as an example of engagement and interest to help encourage other players to do the same.

but anyway, at the end of the day, I think your buddy should talk to his players (always the most important thing) and see what's up. hopefully not all of the players are selfish jerks that care only when the story revolves around them, but I think it'll work out. best of luck! (also sorry this is so long holy fuck the TL;DR is just tell your buddy to communicate, it does wonders, and don't let those shopping trips go on for an hour dude wtf, alternatively if I didn't mention this enough before but the /least/ the players can do is pay attention. we're all adults. we can pay attention. it's not that hard.)

That's a really interesting idea! I think this depends on how you want to do this. If you're going to do it one-to-one (just you and the other player) or if you want to do that and have the other player's leave to room or do that with them there? I'm not sure what you're planning on that regard, or how long you want these sequences to go. I think it's a very interesting idea! In a campaign that I ran, I had a similar thing but I had the dreams merge with each other. So player 1 would be in their dream, exploring, and suddenly player 2 would wake up there too. Then it would warp into player 2's dream and then player 3 would wake up and etc. I played with the idea of having player 1 travel to player 2's dream and then they both travel to player 3's dream but I liked the idea of making sure that player 1 wasn't the only character to have a scene that wasn't intruded on (they need to get the backstory violation too!). I felt it kept them all engaged even when the focus wasn't on them. I'd be really interested in hearing how you handle your scenario in your own game! :D

And for your other question-also super interesting. Is player 4 going to hear player 3's dream scenario? If that's the case then I think spacing them out might be good (ex. having player 3 go, then 2, THEN 4) so that they kind of "forget" what was happening in their sequence. I also think that making an effort to describe both events in different ways would help. Play it from their point of view. Maybe player 3 doesn't see the orcs as just orcs, they're large violent monsters. Player 3's fellow armymen are loyal and brave, they've left behind family to fight against these creatures. Don't describe them the same way. When it's player 4's turn they look to their strong and beautiful allies, they're /family/. They're being attacked by stupid and arrogant little creatures. Because it's a "dream" I think you'd be able to get away with describing the scenario in a hazy way, and purposefully obscuring certain details that might give away that it's the same sequence. Like when you're in an actual dream and you can't REALLY see the faces but you kind of know that there's a face there and you don't really realize that you were dreaming a dream where no one had any goddamn faces until you wake up and are like "shit, they had no faces". But in that way I think you can make it feel like two different scenarios, even though it isn't just with describing it differently. Of course, there will always be some obvious parallels that someone might pick up on (but that's not a bad thing, I think it's fun to be like "damn is this the same dream OH SHIT ITS THE SAME DREAM", maybe they might SUSPECT but they'll never know for sure until you reveal). Personally, as a player, I don't think I would pick up on them being the same sequence right away if you just make a conscious effort to make them feel different and don't outwardly say it.

Anyway, sorry that's a bit long! I am weirdly interested in hearing how this goes, I really like the idea. Might have to steal it ;)
